opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that these aren't competing paths so much as complementary ones, and I'd be worried if the field only pursued one of them.

Foundation models are remarkable. They've distilled an enormous amount of what humans have written and said and drawn, and that's a genuine gift. But it's a particular kind of knowledge: it's knowledge *about* the world as described by people, captured at a moment in time, and then largely frozen. What it isn't, at least not by default, is knowledge that comes from an agent acting in the world, seeing the consequences of its own actions, and adjusting moment by moment.

That second kind of learning is what I've spent a lot of my career on, particularly in rehabilitation robotics and prosthetics. When you're building a prosthetic arm that has to work with one specific person, their body, their muscle signals, the way their habits drift over a day as they get tired, there's no pretrained dataset that tells you that. The system has to learn from that person's raw sensorimotor stream, continually, while it's being used. It has to make predictions about what's coming next and update those predictions as it's surprised. That's reinforcement learning and continual prediction learning in their most natural setting.

So the value I see is a few things. One is adaptivity: the world doesn't stand still, and a system that can only learn offline will always be a little out of date with the particular situation it's in. Another is grounding: an agent that has built up its own predictive understanding of how its actions change its sensations has a kind of understanding that's tied to experience, not just to text. And a third is partnership. If we want machines that genuinely collaborate with people, that adapt to us as we adapt to them, they need to be learning from the interaction itself.

Where it gets really exciting is putting the two together. A foundation model can give an agent a rich prior, a head start, a way to communicate with people. Experiential learning lets that agent refine, specialize, and keep growing once it's out there living alongside us. I think the most capable and the most useful systems of the next decade will be the ones that do both: they start out knowing a lot, and they never stop learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the value is actually enormous, and it comes from the fact that these two approaches are answering fundamentally different questions.

Foundation models are, in a sense, a distillation of human knowledge. They're trained on the record of what people have already written, drawn, and said. That's incredibly powerful, but it's also a snapshot. It's static. It doesn't know what happened in the last five minutes in the room you're standing in, and it has no stake in what happens next.

The thing I've spent most of my career on, going back to my work with Rich Sutton and the group in Alberta, and the work with people using prosthetic limbs, is a different question: how does an agent come to understand its world through its own ongoing stream of experience? Sensations coming in, actions going out, moment by moment, with no one labeling anything. That kind of learning is grounded. The agent's knowledge is tied directly to its own sensors and its own body, and crucially, it keeps updating. If the world changes, or the user changes, or a motor starts to wear out, the agent notices because its predictions start to fail.

That matters a lot in the settings I care about. If you have an amputee wearing a bionic arm, that person is not a generic human. Their muscle signals, their routines, their preferences are theirs alone, and they drift over weeks and months. No amount of pretraining on the internet is going to tell the device what this particular person's shoulder does on a cold morning when they're tired. You have to learn that in situ, continually, from experience.

So I don't see it as either-or. I see foundation models as giving us a tremendous prior. They know what a cup is, what a door is, how people generally talk about things. And then continual, experiential learning is the mechanism by which a system personalizes, adapts, and stays honest with reality. The pretrained model is the starting point. The experiential learner is what keeps the system alive, so to speak.

The other thing I'd say is that experience is the thing that's actually unbounded. We're already hearing people talk about running out of high-quality human data. But the stream of experience an agent gets from interacting with the world never runs out. It's generated fresh every second. If we want systems that keep getting better over the long run, rather than plateauing at the edge of what humans have already written down, I think we have to get serious about learning from that stream.

And honestly, there's a scientific value too. Building agents that learn from raw sensorimotor experience forces us to confront the hard questions about representation, prediction, and what it means to understand something, in a way that scaling up a pretrained model lets you sidestep. Those questions don't go away just because the models got big.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re very complementary. A pretrained model gives you access to an enormous amount of accumulated human knowledge. But there’s also knowledge that comes from interacting with the world: taking an action, seeing what happens, and adjusting what you do next. That’s especially important when an AI system has to work with a particular person, in a particular environment, over time.

Take a prosthetic arm. There’s a lot you might want it to know in advance, but it also needs to learn how you move, what its signals mean as you use it, and how its actions affect you. And you’re learning at the same time. So the challenge isn’t simply to build a system that arrives with the right answers. It’s to build one that can participate in that ongoing process of adaptation.

Learning from sensory and motor experience gives us a way to connect knowledge to consequences. What do I expect to happen? Did it happen? Can I do something differently next time? Foundation models can contribute powerful starting points, while experience allows the system to test and refine its expectations. I see a lot of value in bringing those capabilities together.

sol-6.1.text:
I see those as complementary directions. A pretrained model brings a tremendous amount of knowledge distilled from what people have written and recorded. But an agent also needs to learn what its own actions mean in the situation it actually occupies: what happens when I move, what can I predict, and how does that change as I interact with someone?

A prosthetic arm is a useful example. Knowing a lot about arms doesn’t, by itself, tell you how this particular person wants to use this particular device today. There’s an ongoing process of adaptation. The person is learning, the machine is learning, and the interaction between them matters.

Learning directly from sensory and motor experience gives us a way to build that ongoing adaptation into the system. It can develop predictions grounded in its own experience and update them when circumstances change. The exciting opportunity is to combine that ability with the broad knowledge of foundation models—to have systems that can draw on what’s already been learned while continuing to learn through participation in the world.
